title: Knowledge check — 8 questions
note: Unlocks after the applied activity is submitted. Retakes are free and unlimited.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between collaboration and diagnosis in this module's terms?
options: Collaboration involves stakeholders; diagnosis is done independently by the L&D team
Collaboration accepts the problem statement as given and delivers well against it; diagnosis refuses the problem statement and establishes what is actually happening
Collaboration is appropriate for small requests and diagnosis for large ones
Collaboration is a soft skill and diagnosis is a technical one
questions.explanation: Both can be done well or badly. The distinction is whether the requester's framing survives contact — and L&D is rewarded for the first and unmeasured on the second, which is why diagnosis needs to be a scheduled step rather than a value.

questions.prompt: Why is training a willingness problem described as worse than doing nothing?
options: Because it costs more than other interventions
Because it damages the credibility of the L&D function with senior stakeholders
Because it produces evidence that the problem was addressed — the course ran, attendance was high — which buys the real cause a long period of nobody looking
Because willingness problems always escalate if not addressed immediately
questions.explanation: The cost is real but secondary. The damage is the false negative it creates in the organizational record: a problem now marked as handled.

questions.prompt: What does the money test establish?
options: Whether the intervention is worth its budget
Whether the person could perform correctly if sufficiently motivated — which separates a knowledge gap from everything else
Whether incentives are the primary environmental cause
Whether the request came from a manager with budget authority
questions.explanation: If a large enough reward would produce the behaviour tomorrow, the capability is already there and instruction has nothing to add. C is a plausible-sounding distractor: the test rules knowledge in or out, it doesn't identify which environmental cause applies.

questions.prompt: How does the module treat the 75–80% environmental-causes figure? `[V]`
options: As a well-established empirical finding that should anchor the diagnosis method
As a fabrication that should be discarded entirely
As a number with weak provenance — a round range attributed to a model rather than a study — that is worth holding as a prior and not worth citing as evidence
As accurate for manufacturing environments but not for knowledge work
questions.explanation: Both halves matter. It has the same profile as the learning-pyramid percentages the next module dismantles, so it doesn't belong on a slide. But a prior only has to change which questions you ask first, and this one would do that at 60% or 85%.

questions.prompt: What were the three jobs production time was performing?
options: Quality control, stakeholder management, and budget justification
The economic filter that killed bad requests, the forced SME conversation that produced diagnosis as a by-product, and the rationing that made choosing necessary
Instructional design, content development, and review
Protecting designer headcount, maintaining vendor relationships, and setting expectations
questions.explanation: None of them were assigned; all three were side effects of the cost. Which is why removing the cost removes them silently — nobody decided to stop doing them.

questions.prompt: Why does the module say functions worst at deliberate diagnosis will feel the collapse hardest?
options: Because they have the least experience negotiating with stakeholders
Because they were most dependent on the accidental diagnosis that slow production produced — being bad at this and slow was survivable, being bad at this and fast is not
Because they typically have smaller budgets and less political capital
Because they are more likely to have adopted AI tools early
questions.explanation: The protection was inefficiency. Remove it from a function with no deliberate practice underneath and there is nothing left holding the diagnosis in place.

questions.prompt: What makes a refusal survive contact, according to Lesson 4?
options: Escalating to a sponsor with more authority than the requester
Citing the research base for why training won't address the problem
Naming what you found, what training would and wouldn't do, and what you will own instead
Documenting the refusal formally so the decision is auditable
questions.explanation: The third part is load-bearing. A refusal that concludes in nothing you own is indistinguishable from avoidance, and a requester who can route around you in an afternoon will route around you.

questions.prompt: A learner's diagnosis concludes that the problem belongs to another function and requires nothing from L&D. How should they treat that?
options: As the correct outcome — clean handoffs are the goal of diagnosis
As a legitimate possible conclusion that becomes a warning sign if it is the systematic pattern, since a diagnosis costing you nothing cannot be distinguished from avoidance
As evidence the diagnosis was performed incorrectly and should be redone
As a reason to build the training anyway to preserve the stakeholder relationship
questions.explanation: Any single diagnosis can honestly land there. The module's discipline is about the pattern: if yours always do, the requester's suspicion that this is evasion is better evidenced than your claim that it's rigour.
